description: Lychee is a team of 10th graders attending Research Triangle High School who want to take their passion for STEM to the next level. Members of Lychee have experience doing hackathons, participating in FRC, and developing games in Unity.
summary: Solar storm is a moon based survival interactive game that teaches children aged 7-12 and teenagers aged 13+ about the dangers of an actual solar storm to astronauts and how to keep your crew safe. One can choose storms of differing magnitudes or difficulties, or opt to face the largest flare in the past month. This uses actual data from NASA and the DONKI database. You have to solve the puzzle. The quicker the mass ejection moves, the less time you have. The bigger the flares, the more radiation. If there is a solar particle event, your crew will be stuck in their shelter for longer. You need to collect resources before the storm hits, and create a wall of protection for your water and food. Manage your power and decide if you should go. Every decision you make will cost you a resource. Each storm has a name given from actual NASA images of the sun taken from the SDO and SOHO spacecraft. Children learn about space weather science by getting hands-on. There is also a Space Academy, Glossary, and a Data & Sources page, meaning every fact is linked to something from NASA.
details:
General Information

Solar Storm is a single-page web game that's set at a four-person Moon base. A solar storm is coming, and the player (acting as the commander) has to act fast. Each mission has four phases:

1. Scramble

The commander has to run through a station map and compete short mini games to pick up resources such as a medkit, water, food, and dosimeters. Each thing you pick up is another thing you have to leave, and you choose what consequences you're willing to deal with.

2. Shelter

The supplies you choose are locked with you; everything else is stuck outside. In Junior Mode (7 - 12), the player builds the wall block by block. While you'd want the shield as high as possible, each water or food box that's used to block radiation is one you can't eat or drink from. Live meters show radiation, food and water supplies, health, and other stats to help the player decide what to do.

3. Storm

Each day and night, there's an event that requires a careful response from the player to keep the crew as safe and healthy as possible.

4. Debrief

The user is ranked on a weighted set of metrics from 1 to 3 stars, and the user receives statistics over the course of the storm. Additionally, the science and what NASA would do are listed on the page.

There are two difficulty modes: Junior Astronaut (ages 7-12) uses plain language, a friendly crew, and the hands-on wall builder. Flight Director (13+) uses real units (dose percentages, Kp index, half-angle of the CME) and tighter trade-offs.

How NASA data is used

Storm values come from NASA's DONKI space weather database: coronal mass ejection (CME) speed and angle, flare class, solar energetic particle (SEP) events, and geomagnetic storm Kp index. These drive the difficulty: CME speed sets the scramble time, flare class and SEP events set radiation per day and shelter length. Three storms are saved as fixed DONKI records, with their record IDs shown on screen. A Live mode reads the last 30 days from the DONKI API and builds a mission from the strongest storm, and falls back to a message if the data can't be reached. Pictures of the Sun and of each storm cloud are generated from NASA's SDO and ESA/NASA's SOHO spacecraft through Helioviewer.org. The home page background uses NASA's image library. The Data & Sources screen links the DONKI records, the CCMC CME Scoreboard predictions, and NASA radiation-protection documents used to inform the game.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Most people have never heard of solar particle events, even though they are a main hazard for Artemis crews. The game aims to give young people an intuitive sense of why shielding, warning time and supplies matter, and to show that real mission decisions involve trade-offs. A Space Academy and glossary (Space Words) explain each concept, and a quiz checks understanding.

Creativity and Design

We used a retro pixel style, with hand-drawn pixel sprites in place of emoji, a walkable station map, synthesized sound, and crew characters with personalities. We designed the dose model as a simple educational model, not a NASA dose calculator: it turns real storm numbers into readable game rules.

Tools

HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks), HTML canvas, the Web Audio API, Google Fonts, NASA's DONKI API and open APIs, Helioviewer.org, and the NASA Image and Video Library. No backend. The game runs entirely in the browser.
